Looking at the nature, I mean, the topic in front of us, it entails and encompasses a lot of things which you need to look at, but looking at it, It is in line with the 20 years of celebration and the evolving nature of inclusive governance. For a very long time, and for the existence of 20 years of CRPD, we all agree that CRPD has influenced regional, sub-regional, and national legal systems, constitution, policies, and administrative measures to ensure that persons with disabilities participate in the development within our respective areas. And looking at what is being portrayed to us, it is really an achievement to have persons with disabilities as participants in the process.— is a fundamental principle towards inclusion. But it is unfortunate to note that the representation of persons with disabilities in different decision-making bodies is still a nightmare, whereby few persons with disabilities have made it into the leadership cadre in their respective countries, and the challenge remains even across the global community, even at the UN systems. You find that we don't have directors heading the UN systems, even if for African Union or European, we don't have persons with disabilities heading the most important position. The same applies to our respective countries. Now, that being said, I would use Tanzania as an example to explain what could be done to ensure that we have effective, meaningful representation of persons with disabilities —across the government structures, in the Parliament, executive bodies, in the councils, and the different levels of the decision. For Tanzania, right after ratification of the UN CRPD in the year 2009, we enacted specific disability laws, the one for Tanzania mainland and the other for Tanzania Zanzibar, which put in place and reflect the content of Article 29 of the CRPD. Article 29 CRTPD requires member states to ensure that we put in place measures that will guarantee participation of persons with disabilities in political and public life, but to ensure that persons with disabilities are active members in terms of election, but also in holding offices. For Tanzania, we made sure that Section 51 of the Persons with Disabilities Act, Act Number 9 of 2010, and the Zanzibar Privilege— Rights and Privileges Act also guarantees the participation of persons with disabilities in all democratic processes, in the election, but holding offices. We did not end up there. We made sure that our constitution embraces articles that guarantees participation of persons with disabilities, Article 11 and Article 18, which guarantees freedom of expression for persons with disabilities, and Article Article 20, that the grantees, association of persons with disability, and Article 21, in terms of expression and of their will and opinion. And also we went further to amend the electoral laws, to reform electoral laws, whereby the Election Act, Presidential, Parliamentary, and Councillors' Election Act, Act Number 1 of 2024, It was reformed to ensure that it embraces the content of Article 29 of CRPD by putting in place the favorable environment for persons with disabilities to be able to participate in the electoral processes, but also in the governance process. As a result of those interventions, Tanzania has made notable progress in terms of including persons with disabilities as representatives in different levels of governance. For 3 years consecutively, we have a member person with disability in the cabinet representing us as Deputy Minister, whereby all the issues that are deliberated at the cabinet levels take into account issues of persons with disability. But also we have permanent secretaries or principal secretaries, full 2 persons with disability out of 25 ministries, and the deputy permanent secretaries with disability there too. But we did not end up there. We have executive officers. We have a Solicitor General with albinism. You can imagine a person with albinism heading the prosecution process. At the end of the day, we are granted issues of disability to be catered for. But we have judges and magistrates with disabilities. We have honorable members of parliament with disabilities. We are now The numbers, already from 2010, there were 3, now there are 5 members of parliament in the National Assembly with disabilities. But not only that, we have ambassadors with disabilities. Our ambassador in Geneva, out of 21 ambassadors, 2 of them were persons with disabilities. And we have directors, we have counselors, we have across the government. But it did not come at once. We had to pay the price. We had to get into collective negotiation beginning with the political parties, especially the ruling parties and even the opposition parties, to understand our issues. Sometimes we could force our way through. You need to be bigger. Persons with disabilities, they need to be bigger. They need to be courageous enough to jump all the barriers that may limit having effective representation or having persons with disabilities in the meaningful leadership positions. But also now, looking at what I explained, it is not true that we have all— we have been there. We still have challenges that limit participation of persons with disabilities, ranging from attitudinal barriers, the way persons with disabilities are perceived by the community. So we need to invest more in terms of advocacy, in collaboration with organizations of persons with disabilities, But civil society organizations, we still have that challenge. We need to look on how we can invest, but also we need to invest in terms of leadership development of persons with disability from their young age. But also we need to— because the world is now in the third era of human rights generation, where groups of human rights keeps coming, so we need to identify who are our allies. We need to engage with women to ensure that women with disability They possess all the required criteria and credentials to be able to be voted in by women with disabilities without looking whether he or she has that disability. The challenge is that if at all we dwell that a person can be voted in or need to be measured as a target that a person with disability has to hold office, that is not enough. We need to understand the environment around us. We need to possess the credentials that is required. We need to possess all the qualities that may make people in a given community to vote that person in. We need to ensure that we invest into our people with disability to know their countries, to know— for instance, we are in the UN. We need a person with disability who can deliver by knowing the UN system, the way they work, because disability— We did not stand alone. In conclusion, the home take of which I think we need you all to look at is the member states. We need to come up with strategies that are measurable to ensure that we could have representations of persons with disabilities across the board. We need to invest in terms of empowering organizations of persons with disabilities and persons with disabilities themselves to be able to stand and fight against the barriers because there are barriers that are there to stay. Atidiro barriers cannot end today. As you can name, we have global south, global north, the black, white, women, female, all these are here to stay. So we need to fight against, I mean, to fight through those. Serem Panjo.

Yes, please. Thank you very much. Thank you for sticking to the time. Thank you for your excellent presentation. Our next speaker will be Ms. Ana Carla Pereira. Ms. Ana Carla Pereira is a Director for Equity and Non-Discrimination at DG Justice and Consumers of the EU Commission. Where she is responsible for policies combating discrimination on the grounds of sex, racial or ethnic origin, religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation. Previously, she served as a cabinet expert and employment and social policy advisor to Nicolas Smith, European Commissioner for Jobs and Social Rights. As cabinet expert, she steered flagship initiatives such as the Minimum Wage Directive, the Platform Work Directive, and work on social dialogue. Prior to that, she was head of the Unity in Directorate General Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion at the European Commission, firstly being responsible for skills and qualifications policies and later on for social protection policies. Ms. Pereira, welcome to the panel. The floor is yours.

Thank you, Chair, and good afternoon, everyone. I really would like to start by congratulating the Bureau for putting this so central topic on our agenda because we believe as European Union and European Commission that the participation and representation of people with disabilities in public life and political life is very central to the implementation of the Convention. So I'm really honored to represent here the European Union as a focal point and share our commitment to this very important principle of the Convention. I would like to mention what we are doing in the European Union in this respect, and I would like to start by saying that for us, participation, meaningful participation Participation of persons with disabilities means having participation in the political process, as actually it has been mentioned by my co-panelist. For us, this means that by ensuring participation in the political process, both at EU level and its member states, we are making sure that organizations are not are not just simply consulted, but they share their expertise, their experience, their priorities, and in this way they contribute to policy design, implementation, and monitoring. At the European level, we have the European, the European strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities that was adopted in 2021 and stems until 2030. 2030, and we have recently adopted new measures that reinforce the action under this strategy. And a very important element was actually to consult persons with disabilities, their representatives, and civil society on the preparation of this strategy. So the strategy has three main angles that I would like to refer here, we believe are relevant for this debate. The first is the direct support we give to organizations of persons with disabilities in the EU. We have what we call the Disability Platform, which is an outlet of dialogue between the focal points of the member states with the Commission, which is the focal point for the European Union, and organizations of persons with disabilities and civil society. And this platform meets very regularly throughout the years to discuss the topics and priorities for implementation. We also provide direct financial support, and this year we have channeled €8 million for the support of organizations of Persons with disabilities, and this is just an example because we do this on a yearly basis. And we also make sure that the consultations themselves are accessible and inclusive because, of course, it's necessary that the consultation is in accessible formats, easy-to-read versions, and targeted outreach to organizations representing the diversity of persons with disabilities. The second point I want to mention is what we do to improve participation in political and public life. And to recall that for us, this is not just a matter of disability rights. This is a fundamental issue to ensure an inclusive democratic governance, because we know that when everyone votes, when everyone is represented, that you have vibrant and healthy democracies. So in the EU, we have been working to make this a reality. We are committed to this obligation that the Convention puts upon us, recognizing that persons with disabilities have the right to participate in political and public life on an equal basis with others, whether it's through voting, standing for election, elections or engaging through their representative organizations. We know that we still have challenges ahead, and so this is what we have been working— and I'll share just a few actions that we have recently taken. We have stimulated the use of alternative voting methods. We improved the polling stations' disability, and we have made more accessible electoral materials. And we have studied what has happened in the last elections for the European Parliament, and we are happy to hear from the monitoring and evaluations that there has been progress when it comes to the participation of persons with disabilities. We have also exchanged good good practices through the European Cooperation Network on Elections, and we have developed a guide of good electoral practices as means of guiding all those who are willing to take a step forward. I would like to mention that accessibility is key in this respect, because it's not only about having the legal right but is also making sure that this legal right is a de facto right and a de facto possibility. Accessibility for us remains key for the participation of people with disabilities, and digital participation is essential because we know that inaccessible digital systems and technologies risk creating new forms of exclusion. Digital accessibility, assistive technologies, and the applications of artificial intelligence for persons with disabilities are at the core of our action. I would like to recall we have a European Accessibility Act. This establishes accessibility requirements on a range of key products and services like banking services, ebooks, e-commerce. And we believe that these measures are important not only from a consumer perspective, but also because access to information and communication and digital services are increasingly necessary for civic and political participation. I will end here because I know we are short of time. Just to confirm that we as European Union, as European Commission remain steadfast on our commitment to the Convention, and we are happy to work with all the partners across the globe who wish to pursue this endeavor. Thank you.

Thank you very much. Thank you very much for keeping to time. Thank you, Ms. Pereira, for your contribution. Now it is my honor to present our next panelist. Mr. Dan Rashal. Mr. Rashal has served since 2021 as Commissioner for Equal Rights of Persons with Disabilities at Israel's Ministry of Justice. In this capacity, he leads national policy, regulation, and enforcement efforts to advance the rights, inclusion, and participation of people with disabilities. In line with Israel's domestic legal framework, and the principles of the UN Convention on the Rights of People with Disabilities. His work focuses on strengthening accessibility, equality, and rights-based implementation across government, public bodies, civil society, and the private sector, while also promoting cross-sector and international cooperation on legislation, policy development, regulatory frameworks, and enforcement Mr. Rishal, you have the floor.

Thank you. I am proud to represent the State of Israel and the Commission for Equal Rights of Persons with Disabilities within the Ministry of Justice. My core message today is simple: participation matters, but participation alone is not enough. We should measure success not only by whether persons with disabilities are present in civic spaces, but by whether they are represented in decision-making, can stand for office, can hold public functions, and can influence the policies that shape their lives. That is the shift I hope we can make in this Roundtable, from access to innovation to access to power sharing. This issue is urgent because democratic systems are already under pressure. The UN Disability and Development Report of 2024 shows that persons with disabilities are still being left behind across multiple SDG targets. So disability-inclusive political participation is not a specialist side issue. It is part of rebuilding democratic legitimacy itself. The legal baseline is already robust. Article 29 guarantees political rights on an equal basis with others, including accessible voting procedures, secret ballots, the right to stand for election, to hold office, and to participate in political parties and representative organizations. Article 33 of the Convention, as well as General Comment No. 7, adds that States must closely consult and actively involve persons with disabilities through their representative organizations in implementation and monitoring. And the CRPD Committee's 2025 Day of General Discussion was convened specifically to prepare a future general comment on Article 29, which underlines that this is an implementation priority and is subject to further deliberations such as the one we are having now. The implementation gap is visible across the system. The Special Rapporteur's 2026 report notes that persons with disabilities remain significantly underrepresented in political decision-making, with legal restrictions linked to legal capacity, stigma, inaccessible political environments, lack of accommodation, financial constraints, and limited leadership pathways all playing a role. The UN Disability and Development Report of 2024 adds that persons with disabilities are underrepresented in public service, that about 30% find voting inaccessible, and that in some countries, persons without disabilities are twice as likely to work as legislators, senior officials, or managers. Women with disabilities are especially underrepresented. Available data from various countries suggest that only 3% work as legislators, senior officials, or managers, compared with 4% of women without disabilities. We don't need to start from scratch. Practical reforms are already well understood. What matters is whether states and institutions treat accessibility as a default feature of political life, whether parties create real pathways into leadership, whether reasonable accommodations and disability-related participation costs are funded, and whether representation is supported after entry into office. The central message is that implementation should be systematic. Information must be accessible. Participation pathways must be open. Institutions must be usable in practice. And accountability must be built into implementation. The first, what can be called package, is in line with the CRPD, is for states and election management bodies. Mr. Rahal, you have 1 minute remaining, please. My closing ask is this: let us raise the benchmark. We should no longer be satisfied when persons with disabilities are merely invited into civic and political spaces. We should ask whether they can set agendas, lead institutions, organize collectively, and obtain remedy when their rights are denied. Over the next set period of time, states, civil society and international bodies should be able to point to four deliverables: discriminatory rules removed, accessibility operationalized, leadership pipelines funded, and progress publicly measured. That is what moving from participation to representation should mean in practice. Thank you.

Ladies and gentlemen, I now invite our next panelist to take the floor. Mr. Floyd Morris. Mr. Morris is a professor, a professor in political communication and disability studies and the director of the Center of Disability Studies at the University of West Indies. The first person with a visual disability, he's a blind person, to be promoted to this rank at the institution. He has researched and published extensively on the subject of political communication and disability studies, evidenced by over 30 international publications. Mr. Morris was first appointed as a senator in 1998, becoming the first person, the first blind person in Jamaica to be appointed to the Senate. He was promoted to Minister of State in the Ministry of Labour and Social Security in 2001 and was instrumental in the design and the passage of the Disabilities Act of Jamaica. For his tremendous effort, he was elected to the United Nations Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2020 and re-elected back in 2024. Mr. Morris, you have the floor. 7 minutes, please.

Thank you. Thank you very much, Chairpersons, and I want to acknowledge all the distinguished guests and panelists, including The chairpersons and members of the CRPD Committee led by Ms. Mian Kim. Persons with disabilities are not objects of charity. We have the right to participate in all areas of life as articulated in the CRPD of 2007. This includes the participation of persons with disabilities in public life. 20 years have elapsed since the CRPD was established, and it constitutes a critical juncture for evaluation. During this time, I have been able to look from a vantage point as a member of the CRPD CRPD Committee, and one who was instrumental in leading the negotiations for Jamaica on the CRPD in 2002 to 2007, of which Jamaica was the first country in the world to sign and ratify the treaty in March 2007. I am currently serving on the CRPD Committee and doing my second term. And I must indicate the CRPD Committee constitutes a dedicated body of competent individuals who have been charged to monitor the implementation of the treaty. And here I want to make an appeal on behalf of the Committee to all States Parties to make sure that we honor obligations, financial obligations to the UN, so that the CRPD Committee and other treaty bodies can complete and advance the important work that have been mandated to them. I have personally participated in over 60 country evaluations on the CRPD Committee over the past 6 years, and in this We have seen a number of challenges, including problems with accessibility, problems with access to justice, independent living, deinstitutionalization, inclusive education, access to employment, access to healthcare, social protection, adequate social protection. And there is a commonality that exists between these countries in the evaluation, where persons with disabilities have been absent from the decision-making table. Persons with disabilities need to sit and participate at the decision-making table where it matters to their lives. Limited involvement of persons with disabilities in political representation, exists across the world. There is approximately 46,500 persons at— in national parliaments across the world. And of this, it is estimated that only 1% constitute persons with disabilities, where we have the global population of persons with disabilities representing 16% are 1.3 billion individuals. There therefore exists a disproportionality in terms of representation of persons with disabilities in national parliaments across the world. There needs to be what I regard as a grassroots political model of disability that represents the next frontier of disability advocacy. Persons with disabilities and their families must join together to use their votes to advocate for programs and policies relating to them. When the 16% of the global population of persons with disabilities join with mother, father, children, it mushrooms to over 48% of of the global population. Politicians do not ignore large numbers of organized groups. Persons with disabilities and their families must organize around this noble objective to get things done for them. In conclusion, persons with disabilities need to move from being mere voters to participants at the decision-making table. The power of our vote must become an intrinsic value. We must join with family members for greater empowerment. NGOs and organizations of persons with disabilities must be involved with setting the agenda with grassroots groups of persons with disabilities. Our vote Our vote is power. Our vote can speak. Our vote has value. We must make it matter in the next disability frontier. I thank you very much.

Thank you, Mr. Morris, for your excellent presentation and to stick to the time. Dear delegates, civil society friends, I will now hand over the co-chairmanship back to Mrs. Studdol-Vessiers, who will continue to moderate our meeting today. Over to you, Mrs. Studdol-Vessiers.

Thank you so much, Mr. de Gouveia, for his excellent co-chairing of this roundtable. I now invite our fifth and final panelist, Ms. Janet Charchook, representing Down Syndrome International, to deliver her presentation.. A little bit about her, Ms. Janet Tchartchouk is a self-advocate and motivational speaker from Alberton, Prince Edward Island, Canada. She is Canada's ambassador with Down Syndrome International and a trustee on their board. Her speaking engagements have taken her across the world, and she has spoken to parents, self-advocates, teachers, educators, medical professionals, lawyers, and politicians about the importance of inclusion for everyone in all aspects of their life. Ms. Charczyk lives independently, volunteers in her community, works as a ranch hand at the equine therapy facility, and believes in showing her abilities. Ms. Charczyk, welcome. You have the floor.

Okay, thank you. Thank you, Doug. All right, so my name is Gina Charczyk, and I am from Canada. I am a board member with Down Syndrome International. We are a global network of people with Down syndrome and their families. I want to start with a question. Imagine if this building had no ramp. There would be an outrage. Imagine if there was no sign language, no captions. We will all say this is against the Convention, and we will be right. But right now in this building, most of what is happening is not accessible to me. The long words, the fast speech, and the thick documents. It somehow that does not cause outrage. I want to ask you today, why not? Because if we do not answer that question, we cannot move from participation to representation. We will only move some of us. There are at least 3 barriers for keeping keep people with Down syndrome and intellectual disabilities out of politics and decision-making. Number one, it is the law. Number two is the way the elections are run. And number three is the table where decisions are made. The first barrier is the law. In many countries, people with Down syndrome and intellectual disabilities are not allowed to vote. We are not allowed to run for election. We are not allowed to be politicians. This is because the law treats us as if we cannot make our own decisions. Sometimes a judge decides this. Sometimes a doctor does. Often it happens automatically like that with no way to challenge it. But change is possible. Some countries have done it. In Canada, my country, the federal court decided in 19— 1988 that you cannot take away someone's vote because of a disability. That was almost 40 years ago. So when people say this kind of change is too hard or too soon, I want to say it is too late. And it is definitely long overdue. The second barrier is the way the elections are run. Even when the law says we can vote, elections are often set up in a way that means we cannot really take part. Polling stations are hard to find and hard to get into. Ballot papers are written in language that nobody can understand. Information about voting is really in a way that we can understand. Websites are not accessible. And it is not just voting. It is the campaigns, the debates, the political parties themselves. They are not built for us to take part. For wheelchair users, we now expect ramps. For deaf people, we now expect sign language. But for people with Down syndrome and intellectual disabilities, easy-to-understand information is still treated as optional. It's nice to have. It's something— it's something you do if you have time or money left over. In 2022, Inclusion International and Down Syndrome International published Listen, Include, Respect. It is a global guideline on how to include people with disabilities. So the question is not how, the question is why it is still not happening. The third barrier is the table or decisions are made. This is the most painful barrier because this is the room where we are supposed to be heard. The Convention says that government must consult people with disabilities through our organizations, Article 4.3 and Article 33. Nothing about us without us. But here is our network tells us our members are often not invited at all. Decisions get made about us without us. Laws that affect our lives are written and we never even heard about them until afterwards, and that is not right. And when we, and when we are invited, the meeting is often not designed to take part for us to take part. The papers are too long, the meeting moves too fast, and nobody asks if we understood. So we are in the room, but we cannot really be in the conversation. That is not participation, that is decoration. But it can be different. I know because I've seen it work for firsthand. I am a board member with DSI. I am given materials in plain language and ahead of time. I am allowed to have a support work person with me. I am asked my opinions and I am listened to. That is what real participation looks like, and that is what every government should be doing. So we ask for— we are asking for 3 things from every government in this room. Number 1 is to change every law that takes away our right to vote or to run for election because of our disability, no exceptions. Number 2 is to make easy-to-understand information the default in elections. In laws, in public life. Not a request, it has to be the default. This means that easy read, plain language videos that explain things simply, whatever the person needs to take part. And number 3, governments, when governments consult people with disabilities, you need to include people with Down syndrome and intellectual disabilities. You need to invite us, send us papers that we can read, give us time, and ask us what we think, because we are people first. And then we can actually listen. These three things are not radical. They are what the Convention already says. If a country would never tolerate an inaccessible building, It should never tolerate inaccessible democracy. I think 20 years is long enough of a wait. Thank you very much.

Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, distinguished delegates, dear colleagues and partners, peace and God's blessings be upon you. My name is Fatma Al-Msharbak and I'm from the Ministry of Family Affairs from the United Arab Emirates. Our debate today comes at an important time as we are reviewing what has been achieved achieved after two, two decades have passed to the adoption of the CRPD and what, what awaits us to implement it. And participation does not mean simply having more people or opening the door to dialogue, but it also means that the voices of persons with disabilities are part of setting priorities and making policies and influencing decisions that affect their daily lives. In the United Arab Emirates, we use the expression of people with determination to express the dignity, the ability, and the contribution of persons with disabilities. And this is accompanied by a national program that makes sure to have actual participation in policymaking and setting the services, not simply being users of those services. And there, the civil participation requires very clear requirements. They require information that is easily accessible, that is clearly stated, consultations and representation that reflects the different kinds of disabilities and experience, and safe channels to express opinions, and forces for leadership and for championing courses. And this is all reflected interested in how policies are made, and we make sure that persons with disabilities and their families play an important role in tying policies with lived experiences in terms of legislation, services, education, employment, and social life would be more effective when— microphone has been switched off.
To thank the UAE for their presentation, I now give the floor to El Salvador. El Salvador, you have floor.

Madam Co-chair, distinguished delegations, the subject that brings us here today will determine the future of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, how to open up spaces and turn them into centers for power and political leadership. The state of El Salvador is driving forward a Transformation to break down the bureaucratic walls that have traditionally limited the participation of persons with disabilities through new institutional design. The state has included persons with disabilities in public governance. They do not participate as observers, but they act as decision makers with full abilities to design our new national inclusion policy that is fully in line with the convention. True civic participation requires accessible, universal, and binding channels that go beyond traditional assistentialist approaches with a passive role. We are promoting mechanisms that allow persons with disabilities to make a direct contribution to the formulation, implementation, and assessment of policies and strategies that impact their lives. A tangible example is our administrative institution. Executive board includes, according to a legal mandate, a representative of civil society from the sector with clear rules about voting and quorums that ensures direct, unmediated, and barrier-free participation. Persons with disabilities participate in inter-institutional coordination and oversight, and that strengthens their impact on public policy. This shows that inclusion cannot be limited to symbolic consultation or physical inclusion. It needs to generate real opportunities for persons with disabilities to exercise leadership, to have an impact on public policy, and to make an active contribution to the development of their communities. In this context, we would like to ask the panelists—
I'd like to thank the distinguished delegate from El Salvador for their intervention. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malta. Malta, you have the floor.

Malta thanks the Bureau and all the panelists for this important discussion. At the heart of Malta's approach is the principle of empowerment. Both our National Disability Strategy and National Autism Strategy are built to ensuring that persons with disabilities are able to to participate and lead in public life on an equal basis with others. A key milestone in this regard has been the Personal Autonomy Act, which affirms the legal capacity of all persons and guarantees access to the supports needed to exercise that capacity. This has been essential in enabling genuine participation in civic and political life. Support measures such as personal assistance, assistive technologies, and sign language interpretation services play a crucial role in ensuring accessibility and equal participation. Without these, participation risks remaining theoretical rather than real. Malta has moved beyond consultation towards active involvement. The Engage Committee ensures direct participation in policy and legislative processes alongside statutory representation on key national boards. We have also strengthened accessibility in public consultations through easy-read and plain language materials and targeted engagement sessions. Structured bodies such as the CRPD Council The Consultative Committee for Persons with Intellectual Disabilities and the Maltese Sign Language Council, as well as the Autism Advisory Council, further ensure sustained participation and voice. All these efforts are translating into real representation. Malta remains committed to ensuring that persons with disabilities are—
I'd like to thank the distinguished delegate of Malta. I now invite the representative from an NGO to deliver their statement.

Hola, mi nombre es Jessica Gutiérrez. I am from Argentina and we are working with the organization Women Knocking Down Barriers and the Latin American Justice Group. I'm taking the floor today because clearly we are talking about leadership and participation, but it's necessary necessary for us to talk about the barriers that women with disabilities face when we are simply trying to live or survive. We face various different forms of violence that we have to go through and overcome little by little with support. But that is when we say that power reaches other spaces where our voices need to be heard. For that to happen, there needs to be a process prior to that. Our familiar supports us, but they need to have the tools that they need to be able to support that woman with disabilities. First of all, so that they can get out of their houses, and next, to be able to overcome all of the barriers that they face in education, healthcare, and in every area. And after that, we need a context of civil society organizations that can support and maintain those women in their activities. It's also important that states and organizations at the global and international levels be able to manage the systems needed to ensure that those voices are heard because today being able to be heard is not a privilege that is enjoyed by all women. It's not just about wanting to do it. You also need to generate the spaces and contexts and structures necessary to ensure that the voices of women with disabilities are no longer silenced, to make sure that they are heard and that they are taken into account in decision-making spaces. Leadership, political participation by women with disabilities is possible, but it cannot be possible without first taking into account the barriers and the violence that we face.
I'd like to thank the representative from the NGO. I now give the floor to the representative from the NHRI. You have the floor.

Bismillahirrahmanirrahim. In the name of God, most gracious, most merciful. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, distinguished delegates, distinguished stakeholders, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the National Human Rights Commission in the State of Qatar and to participate in this very important discussion on enhancing civil participation and leadership and advocacy for persons Disabilities in political and public life. The National Human Rights Committee does not, does not deal with the disability file as a simply marginalized one. Rather, it is a fundamental one related to rights and requires permanent attention and renewed interest. And based on this position, the Commission has participated effectively in drafting the Law on Persons with Disabilities No. 22 of the year 2025 and also and we have advocated for adopting it. It is a law that is a qualitative shift towards the rights of persons with disabilities and guaranteeing their full participation in public life. And in recognition of the need for specialization in dealing with persons with disabilities, we've established a specialized unit for persons with disabilities to follow up on their issues regularly and sustainably. And we work diligently to remove any obstacles that may may prevent them from fully enjoying their guaranteed rights. And based on this, the Commission at the end of 2023 hosted the Second National Human Rights Conference under the title Human Rights for Persons with Disabilities: Protection and Empowerment. And we invited specialized experts and organizations from all over the world, and we have issued very valuable recommendations. And as we are committed to transforming these recommendations into tangible procedures. Therefore, we are following the implementation on the ground very diligently. And we must note that challenges still exist because the gap between what laws guarantee and what people actually experience in life requires— these gaps require us to do more work and in more solidarity. Therefore, all governments and international organizations and society must work together. Microphones, please.

Reforms implemented at the national level are fully aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, and future efforts will focus on expanding access to services, enhancing employment and educational opportunities, and advancing the implement—

Distinguished delegates, Estimados panelistas, as we come to close of this important roundtable, I would like to express my sincere gratitude to all panelists and the participants for your contribution throughout these discussions. Today's discussions have demonstrated that participation is not enough if it does not lead to representation. Persons with disabilities must not only be consulted, they must be the present where decisions are made, where policies are shaped, and where the future of our societies is determined. 20 years after the adoption of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, we have witnessed important progress, from legal reforms to guaranteeing accessibility. Still, as many speakers highlighted today, the reality is that persons with disabilities continue to face barriers to voting, standing for elections, accessing public office, participating in civic life, and exercising leadership to their communities. We also heard that accessibility must be understood broadly. A woman with intellectual disability should be able to stand for election because election guidelines are available in plain language that she can read and understand. Refugees with disabilities should be able to influence political party processes because they have been given a seat at the table and a voice in decision-making. A deaf person like me should be able to hold public office without barriers. For example, to be the president of a country, the mayor of a city, a minister, all without barriers because sign language interpreters are recognized as an essential part of the support required to perform that role. As civic space continues to shrink for organizations of persons with disabilities, the principle of nothing about us without us remains as relevant today as ever. Our call today is to increase investments in disability inclusion, strengthen partnership with OPDs, and remove legal, physical communication and attitudinal barriers. This is why the upcoming CRPD General Comment on Article 29 matters for all of us. As I conclude, I reiterate International Disability Alliance's commitment to collaborate with all stakeholders to make representation a reality and ensure that persons with disabilities are fully included in political and public life. Thank you, all of you.

I'd like to thank Mr. Dagobea for his inspiring closing statement. As we wrap up, I would just like to mention some points as a summary from us as co-chairs to yourselves, which will be very helpful, I'm sure, for all of you when you're doing your reporting. So to sum up from this roundtable, various interventions describe the barriers that persons with disabilities face in participating in political and public life. They experience legal and physical barriers to vote and to run for office. They encounter inaccessible political and public environments, and as a result, they are underrepresented in public office and in leadership positions in countries as well as international and regional organizations. It was encouraging to hear about initiatives to address these challenges. The CRPD guarantees participation in political and public life, and we have heard how countries have reflected these guarantees in their national laws. We have heard about persons with disabilities taking positions as members of Parliament, and in other leadership positions. Persons with disabilities and their representative organizations are also being increasingly consulted to design regional and national strategies on disability. Countries have invested in accessible electoral materials and stations and in digital participation. On the way forward, speakers stressed the need to change mindsets and attitudinal barriers towards persons with disabilities. They highlighted the need to develop strategies that are measurable to ensure participation of persons with disabilities, including in policy design and monitoring. And they called for targeted measures to ensure that progress reaches women with disabilities as they face multiple barriers. Thank you all, to panelists and participants, for a productive discussion sharing concrete solutions to enhance accessible civic engagement, leadership, and advocacy democracy and political life.
